extracted.intended_audience: university health education faculty, academic administrators, and researchers interested in faculty grant-writing training and activity
extracted.subtask_short: grant writing for university health educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical findings about faculty grant-writing activity, barriers and incentives, institutional supports, and graduate training in grant writing for university/college health education programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to prepare proposals for external funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduate competencies cite the need for health education professionals to be able to prepare proposals for funding from external sources (National Commission for Health Education Credentialing, 1998; Core Competencies for Public Health Professionals, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a core competency that graduate programs should address; implies programs should teach proposal preparation skills explicitly (no scoring guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived preparedness to write grants (at graduation vs currently)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty self-reported how prepared they felt to write grants immediately following graduate education and how prepared they currently feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key empirical indicators: 23% felt prepared immediately after graduation; ~80% felt currently prepared. Used as an outcome measure of training effectiveness and professional development (measured with Likert-type responses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of grant-writing training
rubrics_metrics.description: Where faculty reported receiving grant writing training: 'through trial and error', 'informally through colleagues', college/university workshops, graduate program, conferences/workshops, professional readings, other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported frequencies: trial-and-error (57%), informally through colleagues (50%), no formal training (37.2%), college/university workshops (34%), in graduate program (27.7%). Use these categories to evaluate how training is obtained and its prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty grant activity level (count and amount)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of grants awarded to faculty in the past 5 years (1-5, 6-10, 11-20, etc.) and grant amount distribution (less than $10,000; $10k-$49,999; $50k-$149,999; etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical benchmark: 88% had at least one grant in past 5 years; majority (59%) awarded 5 or fewer grants; 51% received amounts less than $10,000. Use these numeric bands to classify activity and typical funding ranges in health education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of awarded funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribution of grant sources received by faculty: internal university, federal, state, private, local, other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported proportions: internal university (52.7%), federal (45.4%), state (43.6%), private (36.2%), local (13.9%). Use for evaluating typical funding mixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Services provided by an institutional grants office
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical grant office services reported: conducts searches for grants, conducts grant-related workshops, helps write segments of grants, completes administrative work for grant submission, other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence/absence and service mix as an institutional-capacity metric; reported prevalences: searches (72.7%), workshops (69.5%), helps write grants (58.2%), completes admin work (47.2%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavy teaching loads as barrier to grant writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty-perceived barrier: heavy teaching loads limit ability to write grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most frequently cited barrier (68.1%). Use as a primary institutional constraint to address (e.g., via released time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative or committee assignments as barrier
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty-perceived barrier: administrative or committee assignments reduce time/ability to pursue grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited by 55.3% of faculty; treat as a major time-allocation barrier alongside teaching loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other scholarly/entrepreneurial interests as barrier
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty-perceived barrier: other scholarly or entrepreneurial interests divert effort from grant writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited by 41.8% of respondents; indicates competing professional priorities that reduce grant activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of advance warning of funding opportunities as barrier
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty-perceived barrier: not receiving timely notice of funding opportunities impedes grant submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited by 33.0%; suggests the value of proactive grant-search services and communication channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not being adequately prepared to write grants as barrier
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty-perceived barrier: insufficient preparation/skills in grant writing limits participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited by 28.0%; supports need for formal training and curricular inclusion of grant-writing instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of assistance for proposal submission as barrier
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty-perceived barrier: insufficient assistance with proposal submission processes (administrative help).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited by 27.3%; indicates administrative support (e.g., grant office completing submission paperwork) can remove barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide released time to increase grant activity (institutional incentive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested university action: provide released time to work on grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most-supported solution (72.0%); recommended tactic for institutions wanting to increase faculty grant activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer technical support (grant locating, proposal writing, budgeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested university action: provide technical assistance such as locating grants, proposal preparation, and budgeting help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by 56.4% of respondents; aligns with services offered by grant offices and addresses skill/time barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer personnel support (graduate assistant, secretary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested university action: provide personnel support to faculty for grant tasks (e.g., graduate assistants, secretaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by 56.4%; practical measure to reduce time burden and increase capacity for proposal preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign portion of indirect funds to faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested institutional incentive: assign a portion of indirect (overhead) funds to faculty members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by 48.9%; financial incentive that may motivate or enable faculty grant-seeking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer administrative support (travel funds, equipment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested institutional assistance: provide administrative resources such as travel funds and equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by 46.5%; broad category of institutional investment to support grant-funded activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of grant writing in promotion and tenure
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion to give greater consideration to grant writing during promotion & tenure decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Least-supported institutional change (27.7%); nevertheless presented as an incentive in literature and prior studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental expectation for new faculty to engage in grant writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether departments expect new faculty to be involved in grant writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High prevalence: 81.6% reported their department expects new faculty to engage in grant writing. Use as a cultural/expectational metric influencing early-career behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of obtaining grants for tenure and promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty-rated importance of obtaining grants for tenure and promotion decisions (Likert scale).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority viewed grants as important/very important for tenure (55%) and promotion (60%). Use as an evaluative signal of institutional reward structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graduate student training in grant writing (should be included)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty opinion on whether formal grant writing should be part of graduate education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong consensus: 89.7% said yes. Use as normative guidance for curriculum design—many faculty support formal inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental offering of graduate grant-writing training (required vs elective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether departments offer grant-writing training to graduate students and whether it's required or elective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported: 64.5% offer training; of those, 31.6% as elective, 28.4% as required. Use to assess curricular uptake and formality of instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involving graduate students in faculty grant-writing activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which faculty attempt to involve graduate students in grant-writing activity (apprenticeship/informal learning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported by 63.8% of faculty as an involvement strategy; authors note apprenticeship often via trial-and-error and colleague mentoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparedness of average graduate student in grant writing at graduation
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty perception of how well prepared their average graduate student is to write grants at graduation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less than half perceived students as moderately to very well prepared (46%); many saw students as minimally or not prepared. Use as an outcome metric for graduate curricula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum recommendation: required doctoral course / elective master's course
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors' recommendation that grant writing training should be required in doctoral programs and offered as an elective in master's programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a curricular policy recommendation based on survey findings and prior literature; actionable guideline for program design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative/standing committee model to support grant writing
rubrics_metrics.description: An institutional model where a standing committee offers social support, collaboration, and technical expertise to foster a positive grant-writing environment (Easter & Shultz, 1998).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as an innovative, effective model; treat collaboration and social support as institutional best-practice criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of survey design and measurement (Likert scales, response-maximizing procedures) to assess perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological practices used in the study: 24-item questionnaire with Likert-type scales, closed-format items, content validation by experts, reliability assessed (KR-20, Cronbach's alpha), and multi-wave mailings to maximize response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a template for measuring faculty perceptions and activity: use validated items, appropriate reliability statistics, and follow tailored design methods (e.g., Dillman) to increase response rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived institutional grants-office help vs grant outcomes (correlates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigated relationships between perceived help from grants office and number of grants received, and between perceived current preparation and number of grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: perceived grants-office help did NOT correlate with number of grants (r = -.007, p = .91), but perceived current preparation DID correlate with number of grants (r = .426, p < .001). Use perceived preparation as an indicator correlated with grant success.
